title: He Could Read Tiny Print Clearly, Yet His Own Face in a Mirror Looked Like a Stranger
description:
Myth vs. Neural Mechanism — Joachim Bodamer (1947): Prosopagnosia — Seeing Every Eyelash in 20/20 Focus Yet Failing to Recognize Your Own Face in the Mirror, grounded in Joachim Bodamer (1947) (Archiv für Psychiatrie und Nervenkrankheiten). Empirical findings show that in 1947 at Winnenden Hospital, German neurologist Joachim Bodamer published a landmark 48-page paper (Die Prosop-Agnosie) describing three brain-injured men — led by 24-year-old Patient S. — and coined the term Prosopagnosia from Greek prosopon ('face') + agnosia ('non-recognition').

At the circuit level, this episode examines how primary visual cortex, fusiform face area, auditory cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that patient S. could read tiny print, name furniture, identify flowers, and describe individual parts of a face ('there are two eyes, a nose, and lips') — yet he stared straight at his own mother, his nurses, and his own reflection in a mirror with zero sense of who he was looking at.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Joachim Bodamer (1947). Die Prosop-Agnosie. Archiv für Psychiatrie und Nervenkrankheiten. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00352849
- Hayriye Dilek Akdoğan, Ali Çağlar Turgut, Yaren Akdoğan, Fuyou Guo (2026). The German Neurologist Joachim Bodamer Who Should Be Remembered and His Legacy to Neurology: “Prosopagnosia”. Neurology India. https://doi.org/10.4103/neurol-india.neurol-india-d-25-00972
- Hadyn D. Ellis, Andrew W. Young (1990). Accounting for Delusional Misidentifications. British Journal of Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1192/bjp.157.2.239
